name: SDD-1
tagline: Computer Corporation of America's 1970s ARPANET prototype, the first general distributed relational DBMS.
description: SDD-1 (System for Distributed Databases) was built at Computer Corporation of America in the late 1970s with ARPA funding and described in a 1980 ACM TODS series by James Rothnie, Philip Bernstein, Nathan Goodman and colleagues. It spread a relational database across sites on the ARPANET, with transaction modules planning and coordinating work and data modules storing local fragments. SDD-1 is remembered for two ideas: semijoin-based distributed query optimisation, which ships reduced relations between sites to cut network cost, and timestamp-based concurrency control guided by 'conflict graph' analysis of transaction classes, plus a reliable-network layer for commit. It never became a product, but it shaped the distributed database textbooks and systems that followed, from R* to today's distributed SQL engines.
statusNote: Industrial research prototype (about 1976-1980) at Computer Corporation of America; never sold. Its semijoin and concurrency-control ideas live on in distributed SQL engines.

scale.notes: Data fragments were placed and replicated across geographically separate ARPANET sites.

strengths: Pioneered conflict-graph analysis to cheapen distributed concurrency control
Early end-to-end design for fragmentation, replication and reliable commit across a WAN
Foundational reading for distributed database theory
weaknesses: No surviving code; known only through papers
Designed for 1970s networks where communication dominated all costs
useCases: History and theory of distributed databases
Background reading for distributed query optimisation and concurrency control
notIdealFor: Any practical workload: nothing is available to run
